meta.title: Who really said "Adversity has the effect of eliciting talents which in prosperous circumstances would have lain dormant"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The line is a modern paraphrase, not Horace's words — though the idea traces to a real couplet in his Satires II.8. Here's the verified provenance.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Adversity has the effect of eliciting talents which in prosperous circumstances would have lain dormant'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Horace's words but Horace's idea: a modern paraphrase of a genuine line from Satires II.8. The verified provenance.

answer.label: Not Horace's words — a modern paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: The familiar English sentence appears in no standard translation of Horace, and the quote sites that spread it cite no source — Goodreads even flags it as community-submitted and “not verified.” The genuine Horatian thought is in the Satires (II.8): “res adversae nudare solent, celare secundae” — adversity lays bare a man’s genius, prosperity conceals it. This one-liner is a loose modern paraphrase of that line, reworded and stripped of its context; the idea is Horace’s, the wording is not.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: “sed convivatoris, uti ducis, ingenium res / adversae nudare solent, celare secundae.” — ‘But adverse circumstances are wont to lay bare the genius of a host, as of a general, and prosperous ones to conceal it.’
trail: The sentence is spread by quote aggregators with no source: Goodreads shows it as community-submitted and unverified, while libquotes merely tags it “Epistles” with no book or line.
Carefully-referenced collections omit it entirely: it is not among the sourced Horace quotations at WIST, nor on Wikiquote.
The real parallel is Satires II.8.73–74, “res adversae nudare solent, celare secundae,” preserved in the Latin at The Latin Library and quoted with translation on Wikiquote.
source.excerptNote: The popular English one-liner is a generalised paraphrase of this couplet, stripped of its dinner-party context — Horace is describing how a banquet host, like a commander, reveals his true quality only under duress.

source.rightsNote: The displayed English sentence is an anonymous modern paraphrase with no identifiable translator and no pre-1931 printing we could locate, so we assert no copyright status for it. Horace’s underlying Latin is in the public domain, as are older prose translations of the Satires — but this particular wording is not traceable to any of them.

author.heading: About Horace
author.bio: Quintus Horatius Flaccus — Horace — was the leading Roman lyric poet of the Augustan age, author of the Odes, Satires, Epistles and the Ars Poetica. The son of a freedman, he studied in Athens, fought on the losing side at Philippi, and later won the patronage of Maecenas. His polished verse on friendship, moderation and life’s brevity (“carpe diem” is his coinage) made him one of the most quoted poets in the Western tradition.

The popular English sentence is a modern paraphrase and is not found in this or other standard translations.

misattribution.heading: The misquote
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most-shared “Horace” lines, yet Horace never wrote this sentence. It is a modern paraphrase: the idea is his, the words are not.

items.why: No standard translation of Horace renders any line as “Adversity has the effect of eliciting talents…” The phrasing is expository prose, not verse, and it is absent from referenced collections such as WIST and Wikiquote.
Sites like libquotes assign it to the Epistles with no book or line. The genuine parallel is in the Satires (II.8), not the Epistles.

misattribution.truthLine: The authentic Horatian thought — that hardship reveals the ability prosperity conceals — is Satires II.8.73–74, “res adversae nudare solent, celare secundae,” as recorded on Wikiquote. The popular one-liner is a reworded gloss of it.

context.heading: Where the idea really comes from
lead: Horace’s Satires II.8 is a comic set-piece: the poet Fundanius recounts a disastrous dinner party at the home of the parvenu Nasidienus, where a collapsing wall-hanging and spoiled dishes throw the host into visible panic. In the couplet that later became this “quote,” the guest Balatro consoles him with a maxim — a host, like a general, shows his real quality only when things go wrong: “res adversae nudare solent, celare secundae.”

Lifted out of that dinner-party frame and reworded, the line hardened into a stand-alone aphorism about adversity and hidden talent. The sentiment survives; the specific English wording that circulates today is a paraphrase, not a translation of Horace’s verse.
context.pull: “res adversae nudare solent, celare secundae” — adversity lays bare, prosperity conceals.
